\chapter{Uno... Otro --- Splitting a Pair}
\label{ch:uno-otro}
\hlchaptermodality{263}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say something different about each of two things.}

I can say something different about each of two things.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[uno... otro]{uno... otro — splitting a pair}

\label{lesson:ES-C67-uno-otro}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Un libro} — one book. \emph{Unos libros} — some books.

Now: two books, and you want to say something different about each.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{\textbf{Otro}} — \emph{the other}. Latin \emph{\textbf{alter}}, which did not mean \emph{any other}: it meant \textbf{the other of two}, the second of a pair.

English keeps that sense in \emph{alternative} and \emph{alternate} — one, then the other, back and forth.

And it takes no article. \emph{Otro libro}, never \emph{un otro libro}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one at each end}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Uno}} \emph{es grande,} \emph{\textbf{otro}} \emph{es bueno.} — One is big, the other is good.
\end{quote}

The pattern splits a pair across the two halves of the sentence: \emph{uno} takes the first, \emph{otro} takes the second. Neither needs a noun after it, because the noun was already named or is obvious.

It agrees, like everything else: \emph{una... otra} for two feminine things, \emph{unos... otros} for two groups.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Uno es grande, otro es pequeño}
  \item \emph{una... otra}, \emph{unos... otros}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What goes at the first half, and what at the second? (\emph{\textbf{Uno}}, then \emph{\textbf{otro}}.)

And does \emph{otro} take an article? (\textbf{No.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — picking one, pairing two, refusing both}

\label{lesson:ES-C67-repaso-uno-otro-ninguno}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}There,\textquotedblright{} near you. (\emph{Ahí}.) \textquotedblleft{}Over there,\textquotedblright{} away from us both. (\emph{Allí}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Here is a whole conversation, and it uses everything in this review.

\begin{quote}
— \emph{¿Cuál quieres? ¿Este de \textbf{aquí} o ese de \textbf{ahí}?} — \emph{\textbf{Ni} uno \textbf{ni} otro. Quiero aquel de \textbf{allí}.}
\end{quote}

Take it apart.

\textbf{By distance.} \emph{Aquí}, \emph{ahí}, \emph{allí} — my side, your side, neither side. They line up one for one with \emph{este}, \emph{ese}, \emph{aquel}, because both sets answer the same question: whose side is it on?

\textbf{By pairing.} \emph{\textbf{Uno}} \emph{... \textbf{otro}}. Not \textquotedblleft{}one and any other\textquotedblright{} — \emph{otro} is Latin \emph{alter}, the other of \textbf{two}. It always implies a partner, which is why the pattern splits a pair across the two halves of a sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{By refusing both.} \emph{Ni uno ni otro.}

Count the negatives in the full sentence and English would object: \emph{No quiero ni uno ni otro} has two. Spanish wants both, because \emph{\textbf{ni}} is Latin \emph{nec} and carries its \emph{no} inside it. The \emph{no} on the verb and the \emph{ni} on each item are not fighting; they are agreeing.

That is the same instinct as the pointing words. Spanish would rather mark a thing in every place it can be marked than mark it once and hope. The double negative is not a sloppy extra — it is the language being consistent with itself.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the whole exchange, both turns, at speed
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Otro} is the other of how many? (\textbf{Two}.) Which word carries a \emph{no} already inside it? (\emph{\textbf{Ni}}.) And which place word goes with \emph{aquel}? (\emph{\textbf{Allí}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
